title: Evaluation of Tilt-correction of Anteversion on Anteroposterior Pelvic Radiographs in Total Hip Arthroplasty
question: Does the Tannast symphococcygeal distance method correct acetabular cup anteversion for pelvic tilt on routine post-operative radiographs after hip arthroplasty?

bottom_line.question: Does the Tannast symphococcygeal distance method correct acetabular cup anteversion for pelvic tilt on routine post-operative radiographs after hip arthroplasty?
bottom_line.answer: No. The correction could not be applied in 44% of cases, and where it could be applied, corrected anteversion correlated very poorly with intraoperative navigation (r = -0.07).

provenance.quote: The correction method could not be applied in 44% (31/71) of the cases, chiefly due to difficulties in visualizing the required landmarks. In cases where it could be applied, corrected values correlated very poorly with navigation measurements (r = -0.07).

sections.title: The Problem: Reading Cup Angle from Hip X-rays
sections.markdown:
When a surgeon replaces a hip, one key task is setting the angle of the new socket, called the acetabular cup. A cup set at the wrong angle can wear faster, loosen, pinch against the bone (impingement) or dislocate. Doctors check the cup's position after surgery, usually with a plain front-to-back X-ray of the pelvis, called an **anteroposterior (AP) radiograph**. These X-rays are cheap, quick and low in radiation. They also distort easily.

Two angles describe the cup. Inclination is how steeply it tilts, seen from the front. **Anteversion** is how far the cup opening turns forward. On an X-ray, anteversion is read from the shape of the oval that the cup's rim casts on the film. That makes it sensitive to how the patient is positioned. If the pelvis rocks forward or backward (**pelvic tilt**), the oval changes shape and the anteversion reading changes too, even though the cup has not moved. Inclination is much less affected.

Several methods try to correct for this. One widely cited method comes from Tannast and colleagues. It uses the **symphococcygeal distance (SCD)**: the vertical distance on the X-ray from the top of the pubic symphysis (the joint at the front of the pelvis) to the sacrococcygeal joint (where the tailbone meets the sacrum). Tannast found that this distance tracked pelvic tilt well. The team built charts called nomograms, separate for men and women, that take the SCD and the measured anteversion and give back a "tilt-corrected" anteversion. But Tannast developed the method with tightly standardized X-rays in young patients who had hip impingement or dysplasia. This study asks whether it works on routine X-rays of older hip replacement patients.

sections.title: How They Tested It
sections.markdown:
The authors looked back at one surgeon's primary and revision hip replacements from February 2016 to February 2017. Every operation used an imageless computer navigation system (Intellijoint HIP). A small camera pinned to the pelvis records the pelvis's orientation at the start of surgery and measures the cup angle against that reference. Because of this, the navigation reading reflects the cup's actual orientation in the body and is not affected by imaging or by the pelvis shifting during the operation. This served as the reference standard.

Two weeks after surgery, patients had standing AP X-rays. One researcher, who could not see the navigation values, measured anteversion and the SCD three times on each image and averaged the results. Each image was scaled using the known size of the implanted femoral head. The researcher then read corrected anteversion off Tannast's nomograms. Each hip therefore had three numbers: uncorrected X-ray anteversion, corrected anteversion and navigation anteversion.

sections.title: Could the Correction Be Applied at All?
sections.markdown:
Of 77 eligible cases, six were excluded (one pelvic fracture, five unreadable X-rays), which left 71.

The first problem was applying the method at all. In 31 of the 71 X-rays (44%), the sacrococcygeal joint could not be seen, so the SCD could not be measured. In 9 of the remaining 40, the measurements fell outside the range of the nomograms. The paper says the correction worked on only 31 of 71 cases (44%), but its results section analyzes a correction group of 40 patients, so the paper is inconsistent on this number.

The measurements themselves were highly repeatable. The researcher's three rounds agreed almost perfectly (intraclass correlation 0.99 for both anteversion and SCD).

sections.title: The Correction Pushed Anteversion Too High
sections.markdown:
Where the correction could be applied, it did not bring the X-ray values closer to navigation. It pushed them upward:

- Uncorrected X-ray anteversion: 25.2° on average (standard deviation 7.6°)
- Navigation anteversion: 27.4° (SD 5.7°)
- Corrected anteversion: 36.9° (SD 7.4°)

In every case, the corrected value was higher than both the uncorrected and the navigation value. The correction moved anteversion by an average of 13.5° (p < 0.001) and left it an average of 10.8° away from navigation. Corrected values showed no real relationship with navigation values (Pearson r = -0.07; an r of 0 means no linear relationship and 1 means perfect agreement). Uncorrected X-ray values also correlated weakly with navigation (r = 0.15), but they were off by only 2.2° on average, and the paper found no statistically significant difference between them and navigation. The raw X-ray reading came closer to the navigation value than the "corrected" one did.

sections.title: Why It Matters, Why It Failed, and the Study's Limits
sections.markdown:
Overestimating anteversion carries clinical risk. If a surgeon believes a cup is more anteverted than it really is, the true angle may be too low, which raises the risk of the hip dislocating backward. The authors say corrected values should be interpreted carefully for this reason.

They suggest several reasons the method failed here:

- **Imaging setup.** Tannast's X-rays were taken with patients lying down, at a fixed 1.2 m distance, with a specific beam aim. Routine post-op films are taken lying or standing, aimed at the pubic symphysis, with some variation in distance.
- **Patients.** Tannast's patients averaged 31.7 years old and this study's averaged 63.1, with different hip conditions and anatomy.
- **Unclear measurement details.** Tannast did not say whether "vertical" was measured relative to the pelvis or to the film, or how images were scaled. X-ray magnification can range from 97% to 127%.

The study has limits. It was retrospective and done at a single centre. It also compares X-rays taken after surgery with navigation readings taken during surgery, although this navigation system has shown errors under 3° against X-rays in earlier work.

The authors conclude that the SCD correction could not be applied to many routine X-rays, and where it could, it did not correct anteversion reliably. They advise against using it for hip replacement patients and say a more accurate way to correct for tilt is still needed.

sources.abstract: Despite inaccuracies due to artifact and variations in patient positioning, anteroposterior (AP) radiographs remain the clinical standard for post-operative evaluation of component placement following total hip arthroplasty (THA). However, cup position, specifically anteversion, can be significantly affected by variations in patient positioning on an X-ray. A major cause of such artifact is unaccounted for pelvic tilt. Several methods for correcting the effects of pelvic tilt on radiographic anteversion have been proposed, with varying degrees of accuracy. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the accuracy and reliability of a commonly referenced method for correcting acetabular cup anteversion in a cohort undergoing total hip arthroplasty and determine its appropriateness for use in this population of patients. Radiographs from patients who underwent primary or revision hip arthroplasty between February 2016 and February 2017 were retrospectively reviewed. Corrected anteversion was calculated by measuring the vertical distance between the symphysis pubis and the sacrococcygeal joint, per the method outlined by Tannast et al. This symphococcygeal distance was then applied to Tannast’s nomograms to calculate the magnitude of pelvic tilt. Corrected and uncorrected anteversion values were compared to anteversion values collected intraoperatively using an imageless computer-assisted navigation device. A total of 71 cases were initially eligible for inclusion in the study. The correction method could not be applied in 44% (31/71) of the cases, chiefly due to difficulties in visualizing the required landmarks. In cases where it could be applied, corrected values correlated very poorly with navigation measurements (r = -0.07). Mean corrected anteversion (36.9°, SD: 7.4°) differed from uncorrected anteversion (25.2°, SD: 7.6°) by an average of 13.5° (p<0.001). sources.sec-materials-and-methods-2/p3: Radiographic analysis was performed on standing, two-week post-operative AP radiographs using TraumaCad (version 2.5, Brainlabs, Chicago, IL). Radiographs were scaled using the known diameter of the implanted femoral head. Pelvic tilt (deviation of the anterior pelvic plane (APP) from the coronal reference plane [-]) was estimated using the method described by Tannast et al. [], where the vertical distance between the upper edge of the pubic symphysis to the centre of the sacro-coccygeal joint is measured. In this context, vertical was defined as a line perpendicular to the trans-ischial line, to account for any pelvic obliquity (Figure ).
sources.sec-introduction-1/p3: Pelvic tilt has been a subject of much discussion regarding its effect on radiographic accuracy, as variations in pelvic tilt alter the projection of the pelvis onto the two-dimensional radiograph, introducing error to the measurement of acetabular orientation [-]. This error is generally considered negligible for inclination [], but anteversion is highly susceptible to changes in pelvic tilt since its measurement is based solely on the shape of the ellipsis created by the cup surface on the radiograph []. To account for this projection error, several methods to correct pelvic tilt on radiographs have been presented in the literature [,], but have yet to achieve general acceptance for clinical use. In a recent study, Tannast et al. [] evaluated several proposed measurements and found that the vertical distance from the pubic symphysis to the sacrococcygeal joint (symphococcygeal distance, (SCD)) correlated well with pelvic tilt. Using this method, the authors developed a nomogram for easy calculation of “tilt-corrected anteversion”. However, the broad application of their preferred method may be difficult, as their radiographic methods were highly standardized and deviate from standard clinical procedure. Furthermore, as they used a cohort of young patients, the validity of their correction method in an older population undergoing THA is in question.
sources.sec-materials-and-methods-2/p4: Anteversion was measured using the trans-ischial line method. All radiographic measurements were made in triplicate and the results averaged to provide a final value. After completing radiographic measurements, the gender-specific nomograms created by Tannast et al. were used to find the tilt-corrected anteversion. The nomograms correlate the SCD with the measured (uncorrected) anteversion to determine the tilt-corrected value. The measurements and application of the nomogram were completed by a single researcher (JV), who was blinded to navigation values.
